beats.text: Before collecting requirements, find the real problem. The fishbone, or Ishikawa, diagram puts the problem at the head, on the right.
Four to eight main causes become the bones. Sub-causes attach to them, often from a brainstorming session. The goal: the root cause.
Research: journals, books, and websites of similar projects.
Observation: watch people at work. The data is very reliable, but people may act differently when watched.
Prototyping: a small working model for users to try. But users may develop unrealistic expectations.
Questionnaires: cheap, anonymous, and fast for many people. Open-ended questions let people answer freely. Closed-ended ones offer fixed choices. The downside: a low return rate.
Interviews: face to face. Unstructured, with only a general goal, or structured, with a fixed set of questions. Rich, but time-consuming.

Sampling collects representative documents and forms. Random sampling picks by pure chance. Systematic sampling picks every x over n-th: one hundred from a thousand means every tenth. Stratified sampling splits into subgroups first.
And Joint Requirements Planning: a workshop of users, managers and I T staff, led by a facilitator, with a sponsor from top management.
